options.text: The summary is the same, and the run costs more: each repeat is a new reader with its own input.
options.why: Right. Each repeat starts a reader that reads the same note again. The harness does not refuse it, so the bill grows and the answer does not change.

options.text: The repeats disagree with the first readers, so the summary is wrong.
options.why: Tempting. The readers read the same file. They agree, and nothing in the run compares them.

options.text: Sub-agents run in parallel for free, so the cost stays the same.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. A sub-agent is another loop with its own turns and its own input. Parallel does not make it free.

outcome: The summary matches the notes. The run started its readers again for notes it had already read, and it cost more for the same answer.
question: A parent has three notes. It starts a reader for each, then starts a reader again for each note. What happens to the summary, and what happens to the cost?

options.text: It makes the work look bigger in a demo.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. The reason has to be about the work, not the picture.

options.text: It keeps a long, noisy search out of the parent's context, so the parent keeps its room.
options.why: Right. Context isolation is one of the two honest reasons: a separate context for a separate piece of work.

options.text: It lets two agents make a shared decision without talking to each other.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. Agents that share decisions implicitly disagree in ways no one sees.

question: Which is an honest reason to add a sub-agent?

options.text: The evaluator approves its own style of work.
options.why: Right. An evaluator that shares the generator's habits passes its work. Its criteria must come from outside the loop.

options.text: The two agents need too much memory to run.
options.why: Tempting. Memory matters less than shared blind spots in this shape.

options.text: The loop costs nothing, because each side is short.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. Each turn of the loop is a model call, so every round costs more.

question: A generator and an evaluator run in a loop. What failure should you watch for?

options.text: An isolated context, so it is cheaper.
options.why: Tempting. Isolated is cheaper, but it cannot see the messages the decision depends on.

options.text: A forked context, so it starts from the parent's messages.
options.why: Right. The forked sub-agent carries the messages, so its first request is larger, and it has what it needs.

options.text: No context at all, and the brief alone.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. The brief alone is what an isolated context gets, and it is missing the thread.

question: A sub-agent must judge a decision that depends on the parent's last ten messages. Which context does it need?

options.text: Treat the silence as a finding that nothing was there.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. A timeout is a failure of the reader, and the parent has learnt nothing.

options.text: Decide with what it has, and say which note is missing.
options.why: Right. A multi-agent system fails in parts. The parent must say what it could not learn and what it did.

options.text: Start the same reader again with no limit.
options.why: Tempting. That repeats the sprawl with no cap, the failure this module starts from.

question: A sub-agent times out and returns nothing. What should the parent do?

options.text: Find something useful in the notes.
options.why: Tempting and vague. Nothing in the result can be checked against that.

options.text: Read notes/a.txt. Return the date as 'date: value'.
options.why: Right. A named file and a named field let the parent check the result line by line.

options.text: Do whatever is needed and report back.
options.why: Tempting and wrong. A brief with no result format gives the parent nothing to check.

question: Which brief lets the parent check the result when it comes back?
